norm.ms: Alert, oriented, follows commands. Speech fluent and clear, understands and repeats normally.
norm.cn1: Identifies coffee and peppermint with each nostril.
norm.cn2: Acuity normal. Visual fields full to finger counting in all four quadrants, each eye.
norm.pupil: Pupils equal, round, briskly reactive to light (direct and consensual).
norm.eom: Eyes move fully in all directions, no double vision, no nystagmus. No ptosis.
norm.cn5: Light touch and pinprick normal on forehead, cheek and jaw both sides. Jaw clench strong. Corneal reflex present.
norm.cn7: Face symmetric: raises eyebrows, closes eyes tight, smiles and puffs cheeks equally.
norm.cn8: Hears finger rub equally in both ears.
norm.cn9: Voice normal. Palate rises evenly, uvula midline, gag present.
norm.cn11: Shoulder shrug and head turn strong both sides.
norm.cn12: Tongue sticks out in the midline, no wasting or twitching.
norm.gait: Walks normally, can tandem walk heel to toe.
norm.romberg: Steady with feet together and eyes closed (Romberg negative).
norm.str_a: 5/5, full strength in shoulder, elbow, wrist and fingers.
norm.str_l: 5/5, full strength in hip, knee and ankle.
norm.tone: Normal tone and muscle bulk. No twitching.
norm.bab: Big toe curls down (flexor plantar response: normal).
norm.vib: Feels vibration and joint position normally.
norm.crd_a: Finger-to-nose smooth and accurate, rapid alternating movements normal.

cases.cc: 62-year-old with high blood pressure woke up with his right side weak. No headache.

f.cn7: Right lower face droops when he smiles; he can still wrinkle his forehead on both sides (forehead spared).
f.str.ra: 3/5 right arm, worse in the extensors (triceps, wrist extension).
f.str.rl: 3/5 right leg, worse in the flexors (hip flexion, ankle dorsiflexion).
f.tone.ra: Increased tone, catch on fast stretch (early spasticity).
f.ref.rl: Knee 3+ with spread, ankle 3+ with 3 beats of clonus.
f.bab.rl: Big toe goes UP and toes fan out (Babinski sign).
f.gait: Swings the stiff right leg out in an arc (circumduction).

cases.why: Face, arm and leg all weak on one side with upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes, Babinski) and NO sensory, speech, vision or thinking problems = a pure motor stroke. The posterior limb of the internal capsule packs the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres tightly, so one small lacunar infarct (lenticulostriate artery, linked to hypertension) hits all three. It's the LEFT capsule because the pathway crosses at the medullary pyramids. Forehead sparing tells you it's an upper motor neuron facial weakness: the forehead gets input from both hemispheres.

cases.cc: 16-year-old woke up and couldn't close his right eye. Drink dribbles from the right side of his mouth. Ear ached yesterday.

f.cn7: Whole right face is flat: can't raise the right eyebrow, can't close the right eye fully (the eye rolls up when he tries, Bell's phenomenon), mouth droops right.
f.cn5: Sensation normal on both sides. Corneal reflex: he feels it in the right eye but the right eye doesn't blink (the left one does).
f.cn8: Hearing equal, but sounds seem uncomfortably loud on the right (hyperacusis).

opts: Right facial nerve (peripheral, lower motor neuron)
cases.why: Whole half of the face weak, forehead INCLUDED, with nothing else abnormal = a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve itself: Bell's palsy. The forehead is involved because the nerve carries every fibre to that side of the face after the nucleus. Loud sounds (stapedius muscle) and a missing blink with intact feeling (CN V senses it, CN VII can't close the lid) fit. Treatment: corticosteroids early, protect the eye with drops and taping at night; most recover over weeks to months.

cases.cc: 45-year-old with the worst headache of her life. Her left eyelid is drooping and she sees double.

f.eom: Left eye rests down and out. It can't look up, down or in. Left lid droops (ptosis). Double vision in most directions. Right eye moves normally.
f.pupil: Left pupil large (dilated) and doesn't react to light. Right pupil normal.

cases.why: Down-and-out eye + ptosis + blown pupil = a complete third nerve palsy. The eye is pulled down and out by the two muscles CN III doesn't supply (lateral rectus, CN VI, and superior oblique, CN IV). The pupil fibres run on the OUTSIDE of the nerve, so compression (here a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, with thunderclap headache) dilates the pupil early. A diabetic third nerve palsy usually spares the pupil because it damages the inside of the nerve. A 'blown pupil' with headache is an emergency: CT angiography, then coiling or clipping by neurosurgery.

cases.cc: Teen with a headache that's worse lying down and in the morning. Now sees double when looking to the right.

f.eom: Right eye can't move outward past the midline when he looks right. Horizontal double vision, worst looking right, gone looking left.
f.cn2: Acuity normal, fields full. Fundoscopy: both optic discs swollen (papilloedema).

opts: Right abducens nerve (CN VI), from raised pressure
cases.why: Can't abduct one eye + horizontal double vision worse looking toward that side = sixth nerve palsy (the lateral rectus is weak). CN VI has the longest course inside the skull, so raised intracranial pressure stretches it: a 'false localising sign'. Papilloedema and a morning, lying-down headache point to raised ICP (tumour, hydrocephalus, idiopathic intracranial hypertension). Needs urgent imaging before any lumbar puncture.

cases.cc: Teen was stabbed in the back on the right side. Now his right leg is weak.

f.vib.rl: Can't feel the tuning fork or tell if his right toe is moved up or down.
f.pt.ll: Can't feel pinprick or cold in the LEFT leg, up to just below the belly button.

opts: Right half of the spinal cord, around T10
Left half of the spinal cord, around T10
cases.why: Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection). Same side: weakness with UMN signs (corticospinal tract, crossed already in the medulla) and loss of vibration/position (dorsal columns, cross in the medulla). Opposite side: loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract crosses within 1–2 segments of entering the cord), starting a level or two below the injury. Arms normal = lesion below the cervical cord; level near the umbilicus = T10.

cases.cc: Woman can't walk straight; keeps veering to the right and knocked over her cup reaching for it with her right hand.

f.crd.ra: Right finger-to-nose overshoots and shakes more as she nears the target (intention tremor, dysmetria). Rapid alternating hand movements clumsy on the right (dysdiadochokinesia).
f.crd.rl: Right heel wobbles all over the shin.
f.gait: Wide-based, staggers and falls toward the right. Can't tandem walk.
f.eom: Full movements, but jerky nystagmus when she looks to the right.
f.tone.ra: Floppy, reduced tone in the right arm.
f.romberg: Unsteady with feet together even with her eyes OPEN, no worse when they close.
f.ms: Alert, oriented. Speech a bit slurred and scanning (syllables evenly separated).

cases.why: Ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus, low tone and scanning speech with normal strength and sensation = cerebellum. The cerebellar hemispheres control the SAME side of the body (the pathway crosses twice), so right-sided signs = right hemisphere. Romberg is about sensory ataxia: a cerebellar patient is unsteady with eyes open too, so the test doesn't point to the dorsal columns here. Causes: stroke, bleed, tumour, MS.

cases.cc: Man had sudden spinning dizziness, vomiting and trouble swallowing. His voice is hoarse.

f.cn5: Can't feel pinprick or cold on the LEFT side of the face. Light touch OK. Left corneal reflex reduced.
f.pt.ra: Can't feel pinprick or cold in the RIGHT arm.
f.pt.rl: Can't feel pinprick or cold in the RIGHT leg.
f.cn9: Hoarse voice. Palate rises on the right only; uvula pulled to the RIGHT. Gag weak on the left.
f.eom: Full movements with nystagmus. Left eyelid slightly droopy.
f.pupil: Left pupil smaller than the right (both react). Left face doesn't sweat (Horner's).

cases.why: Crossed findings (face on one side, body on the other) = brainstem. Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome, usually a vertebral or PICA occlusion: left spinal trigeminal nucleus (left face pain/temp), spinothalamic tract that already crossed (right body pain/temp), nucleus ambiguus (CN IX/X: hoarseness, dysphagia, uvula deviates AWAY from the weak side), descending sympathetic fibres (left Horner's), inferior cerebellar peduncle (left ataxia), vestibular nuclei (vertigo, nystagmus). Strength is normal because the pyramids are in the MEDIAL medulla.

cases.cc: 58-year-old with type 2 diabetes for 15 years. Feet feel numb and burn at night.

f.pt.rl: Pinprick reduced in a 'stocking' up to mid-shin.
f.pt.ll: Pinprick reduced in a 'stocking' up to mid-shin.
f.vib.rl: Can't feel vibration at the big toe or ankle; position sense reduced at the toe.
f.vib.ll: Can't feel vibration at the big toe or ankle; position sense reduced at the toe.
f.pt.ra: Slightly reduced at the fingertips only.
f.pt.la: Slightly reduced at the fingertips only.
f.romberg: Steady with eyes open, sways and nearly falls with eyes CLOSED (Romberg positive).

cases.why: Symmetric 'stocking-glove' sensory loss starting in the longest nerves (toes first, fingers later), lost ankle reflexes and a positive Romberg = a length-dependent peripheral polyneuropathy. Diabetes is the commonest cause: high glucose damages small fibres (burning, pain/temp) and large fibres (vibration, position, reflexes). Romberg is positive because the brain lost position sense from the feet and needs the eyes to balance. Treatment: glucose control, foot checks, and nerve-pain drugs (e.g. gabapentinoids, SNRIs).

cases.cc: College student had diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. Over 3 days his legs got weak, now his hands too.

f.pt.rl: Mild tingling in the toes, pinprick nearly normal.
f.pt.ll: Mild tingling in the toes, pinprick nearly normal.
f.cn7: Both sides of the face mildly weak (can't bury eyelashes fully).

opts: Peripheral nerves and nerve roots (acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy)
cases.why: Rapidly ascending symmetric weakness, LOST reflexes everywhere, mild sensory symptoms and bilateral facial weakness after an infection (often Campylobacter) = Guillain-Barré syndrome. Antibodies made against the bug cross-react with myelin on peripheral nerves and roots (molecular mimicry). Lost reflexes separate it from a cord lesion (which gives brisk reflexes and a sensory level once spinal shock wears off). Danger: breathing muscles, so lung capacity is checked often. Treatment: IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.

cases.cc: Teen girl's eyelids droop by evening and she sees double after reading. Chewing gets tiring.

f.eom: Starts normal. After looking up for 60 seconds her lids droop and she reports double vision; changes from test to test. Pupils not involved.
f.str.ra: 5/5 at first, but shoulder abduction fades to 4/5 after 10 repeated pushes.
f.str.la: 5/5 at first, fades to 4/5 after repeated pushes.
f.cn9: Voice gets nasal after counting out loud to 50.
f.cn7: Mild weakness closing the eyes tight; can't hold cheeks puffed for long.

cases.why: Weakness that FATIGUES with use and changes from minute to minute, eye and bulbar muscles first, normal reflexes, normal sensation, normal pupils = myasthenia gravis. Antibodies block or destroy acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, so each repeated nerve impulse works less well. Pupils are spared (that's a different, autonomic type of synapse). Diagnosis: acetylcholine receptor antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation, CT chest for a thymoma. Treatment: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine), immunosuppression, thymectomy.

cases.cc: 50-year-old dropping things, with twitching muscles in his arms and slurred speech for a few months. No numbness.

f.tone.ra: Wasted hand muscles with visible twitches (fasciculations), but tone increased at the elbow.
f.cn12: Tongue wasted and wriggling with fasciculations.
f.ms: Thinking normal. Speech slurred and slow (dysarthria).

opts: Upper AND lower motor neurons (motor neuron disease)
cases.why: Wasting + fasciculations (lower motor neuron) in the same limbs as brisk reflexes + Babinski (upper motor neuron), with completely normal sensation and no eye or bladder trouble = amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a motor neuron disease. Both motor neurons degenerate; sensory pathways are spared, which rules out a cord compression or neuropathy. Riluzole and edaravone modestly slow it; care is multidisciplinary (breathing, feeding, communication).

cases.cc: Teen keeps bumping into doorframes on both sides. Grew 8 cm this year and his shoes keep getting tight.

f.cn2: Acuity normal. Visual fields: can't see the OUTER half of the world with either eye (bitemporal hemianopia). Inner halves fine.

opts: Both optic nerves in the orbits
cases.why: Losing both outer (temporal) fields = the crossing fibres in the middle of the optic chiasm are damaged. Those fibres come from the nasal half of each retina, which sees the temporal world. A pituitary tumour pushing up from below is the classic cause; growth spurt and growing feet suggest a growth-hormone-secreting adenoma (gigantism before the growth plates close, acromegaly after). Treatment: transsphenoidal surgery through the nose, a neurosurgical classic.

cases.cc: Older woman bumps into things on her right side and thinks her glasses are wrong. No weakness.

f.cn2: Acuity normal. Visual fields: can't see the RIGHT half of the world with either eye, but the very centre is spared (right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing).
f.pupil: Pupils equal and reactive (the light reflex pathway branches off before the visual cortex).

cases.why: Same half of the world missing in both eyes = behind the chiasm. Right field = LEFT brain. Sparing the centre (macular sparing) and normal pupils point to the occipital cortex, usually a left posterior cerebral artery stroke; the occipital pole often gets extra blood from the MCA. No weakness or sensory loss, so the motor and sensory pathways are fine.

cases.cc: Man had surgery on the left side of his neck. Now his speech is a bit clumsy.

f.cn12: Tongue points to the LEFT when stuck out. Left half of the tongue is thin and wrinkled with fasciculations.
f.ms: Alert. Slight trouble with 'l' and 't' sounds.

cases.why: The genioglossus muscles PUSH the tongue out. If the left one is weak, the healthy right side pushes the tongue toward the weak LEFT side: 'the tongue licks the lesion'. Wasting and fasciculations make it lower motor neuron, i.e. the nerve itself, which runs near the carotid in the neck and can be injured during carotid surgery.

cases.cc: Man with severe low back pain now can't pee and his legs are weak. Numb where he'd sit on a saddle.

f.pt.rl: Numb over the back of both thighs and the inner buttocks (the 'saddle' area).
f.pt.ll: Numb over the back of both thighs and the inner buttocks (the 'saddle' area).

cases.why: Below L1–L2 there's no cord, only the cauda equina (a bundle of nerve roots). Compressing them gives LOWER motor neuron signs in both legs (floppy, weak, lost ankle reflexes, no Babinski), saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention. A big central disc herniation is the usual cause. It's a neurosurgical emergency: MRI and decompression within hours to save bladder and leg function.

cases.cc: Woman's family says she 'ignores' her left side. She eats food only from the right of her plate.

f.ms: Alert. Denies anything is wrong with her left arm (anosognosia). Draws a clock with all the numbers crammed on the right side.
f.pt.la: Feels pinprick on the left arm, but when both arms are touched at once she only reports the right (sensory extinction). Can't identify a coin in her left hand by feel (astereognosis).
f.vib.la: Vibration normal; position sense slightly off.
f.cn2: Ignores the left side of the room. When each half-field is tested alone she sees it; both at once she misses the left (visual extinction).

cases.why: Hemineglect, denial of the deficit, extinction to double stimulation and astereognosis with only mild weakness = cortical sensory/attention signs of the NON-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe. The right parietal lobe attends to both sides of space, the left mostly to the right, so right parietal damage leaves the left half of the world 'unattended'. Usually a right MCA stroke.
